source.title: Reversion, Retention, and Semantic Intervention: Measuring Functional Content in CLIP Fine-Tuning Deltas
source.authors: Chih-Ting Liao; Ke-Zhen Bao; Xin-Zhuo Cao

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It pairs component reversion with component retention to compare removal costs with recoverable task performance, conceptually testing whether ablation-only importance can miss a component’s functional contribution. It does not use the original language-model layer-ablation method, and studies CLIP fine-tuning deltas.
record.gate_note: The paper measures component-level reversion costs and retention recovery, relevant to V7. It does not measure later attention components changing their outputs after an ablation, nor the specific mechanisms or settings in V1–V6. Semantic readout counts, direction-surgery results, random-subset comparisons, and prediction-agreement results do not measure one of the tested claim versions and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: No claim version is tested. The study reverts or retains fine-tuning weight deltas in CLIP vision transformers and compares removal cost with retained recovery. It never measures downstream components changing their outputs after an ablation, which is what self-repair is. The system is also not a language model. The authors call the result 'operational redundancy' (overlapping recovered behaviour) and say outright that they do not demonstrate a downstream compensation mechanism. Hydra and Rushing & Nanda are cited only in related work. V7 names a consequence 'because of self-repair'. This study shows that reversion cost understates contribution, but because of redundancy among jointly trained update groups, not measured self-repair. That is a related but different construct, so it goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a small reversion cost can coexist with substantial retained recovery, which they call operational redundancy. They add that VO retention beats count-matched random subsets and that VO and MLP retentions correct overlapping errors. Margins reveal contributions that accuracy hides, and readout-guided direction removal cuts recovery more than random removal. They confine all claims to this CLIP fine-tuning recipe and do not claim a self-repair mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weight-level reversion and retention of fine-tuned CLIP visual-block update groups, with accuracy, loss, and margin measures. It does not perform the original language-model attention-layer ablation and downstream-output analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary across task/dataset, component (VO versus MLP), model size, and metric (accuracy, cross-entropy, correct-class margin).

fits_no_version.finding: In CLIP ViT-L/14 and ViT-B/16, reverting VO fine-tuning deltas costs little accuracy (0.000 on Charts, 0.010 on EuroSAT). Retaining VO deltas alone recovers 0.43–0.87 of the accuracy gain, and VO and MLP retentions jointly correct 25–81% of pretrained errors. Correct-class margin still drops after every VO reversion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Operational redundancy of fine-tuning updates: removal (reversion) cost of a jointly trained update group understates its recoverable contribution, because other update groups support overlapping behaviour; the understatement depends on task and metric (accuracy vs loss vs margin).

record.problems: Evidence is limited to five CLIP classification setups using a shared fine-tuning recipe and the final six visual blocks; it does not establish downstream self-repair. Bootstrap intervals are conditional on the trained checkpoints. The paper notes that component updates were trained jointly and that retention measures recovery through the shared pretrained network, not identical internal computation. Direction surgery can remove pretrained mass and is not direction-only retention. GPU training and intervention runs were not repeated during packaging.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, no eligible component reversion/retention result for the tested V7 version was omitted. Results on QK components, random masks, semantic readout, direction surgery, and prediction agreement were left out because they do not measure V7's component-ablation versus retained-recovery comparison.

untested.parts: Not tested at all: no attention-layer ablation in LMs and no measurement of later-layer compensation.
Not tested at all: no late-MLP erasure of the maximum-likelihood token.
Not tested at all: no single-head ablation on general text.
Not tested at all: no per-prompt compensation distribution and no overcorrection measure.
Not tested at all: no backup heads, copy suppression, LayerNorm rescaling or anti-erasure neurons.
Not tested at all: only weight reversion to pretrained values; no mean or resample ablations.
Not tested: no ablation-based attribution in LMs is shown to be misstated because of measured self-repair. The understatement shown here comes from redundancy among fine-tuning deltas in CLIP.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled V7 as tested with supports and limits_scope labels; both labels are removed. The study's object is weight deltas, not activations, and its system is CLIP vision, not LMs. It never measures compensation by downstream components. The authors only remark that downstream computation 'can compensate' in principle. Retention rows were marked 'partial', which is meaningless for any version. The pre-specified dissociation hypothesis failed, as the authors report. Table 9 (joint corrections) and Table 4 (random-mask controls) would be needed if the fits_no_version claim is adopted.

versions.untested_parts: Layer ablation followed by compensation from later attention layers and restoration of the original output.
Late-MLP downregulation of the maximum-likelihood token and its change after earlier-component ablation.
Single attention-head ablations, full-distribution compensation on general text, and breadth across language-model families and sizes.
Prompt-level variability, average compensation, and overcorrection.
Backup heads, copy-suppression heads, final LayerNorm rescaling, or anti-erasure neurons as mechanisms.
Comparison of mean/resample ablations with zero ablation.

Tests component reversion versus retained recovery in CLIP classification, not whether downstream computation itself changes to restore predictions or whether language-model ablation-based scores are affected.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Charts and EuroSAT component-level accuracy and loss comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Low VO reversion costs coexist with substantial retained recovery; the paired results show that reversion cost alone can understate recoverable adaptation (r01-r02, r05-r06, r25-r26, r29-r30).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Flowers102, Aircraft, and Flowers102 ViT-B/16; and continuous-margin measures
reader_labels.reason: Recovery is incomplete, some settings have appreciable reversion costs, and margin recovery/cost differs from accuracy, so the discrepancy depends on task, component, and metric (r13-r24, r37-r48, r49-r60).
